claims.text: Localized grain-boundary and interfacial strains govern the magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Localized grain-boundary and interfacial strains govern hysteresis during low-field magnetic cycling.
These strains act by modulating the energy barrier for a first-order magnetostructural transition.
The relevant as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys are rapidly solidified materials exemplified by arc-melted ingots or melt-spun ribbons.
The initial alloy forms a single-phase ordered hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited material has a high density of grain boundaries.
The as-deposited material contains heterogeneous strain fields.
Controlled post-deposition annealing is proposed to relieve internal strain and change grain-boundary density through stress relaxation and grain growth.
The first-order magnetostructural transition occurs near room temperature under applied fields around 1 T.
Annealing-induced strain relief narrows the distribution of local transition temperatures.
Annealing-induced strain relief lowers the energy barriers for the magnetostructural transition.
A narrower distribution of local transition temperatures produces a broader, less sharp magnetic-entropy-change profile.
Lower transition barriers reduce hysteretic losses during low-field cycling.
Altered grain-boundary characteristics change domain-wall dynamics and transition kinetics.
Annealed samples will have a lower hysteresis-loop area than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will have a broader magnetocaloric transition profile than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will show a modest reduction in peak magnetic entropy change.
The sharp, hysteretic transition in the baseline is caused by high interfacial strain and a dense grain-boundary network.
The predicted behavior applies across similar non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi compositions made under comparable rapid-solidification conditions and tested at low fields.
The prediction may fail when severe annealing causes phase segregation or unwanted secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says annealing narrows the distribution of local transition temperatures but then predicts a broader, less sharp transition. Without an additional broadening mechanism, narrowing a transition-temperature distribution would ordinarily imply a sharper profile.

The baseline attributes a sharp transition to heterogeneous strain and dense interfaces, while the mechanism associates removal of that heterogeneity and narrowing of local transition temperatures with broadening. These causal descriptions are internally inconsistent.

The material is called as-deposited and the treatment post-deposition, but arc-melted ingots are given as an example of the initial state even though conventional arc melting is not a deposition process and is not generally classified as rapid solidification.
